meta.description: Composites manufacturing process capability matrix for AI-assisted process selection
meta.notes: Values are representative industry ranges. Actual results depend on specific materials, tooling, operator skill, and environmental conditions. Always verify against material supplier datasheets and process specifications.

processes.name: Wet Layup / Hand Layup
processes.description: Dry fabric + liquid resin applied by hand with brush/roller onto an open mould. The simplest and most accessible composites manufacturing method.

capabilities.surface_quality_notes: One good surface (mould side); bag/free side is rough and resin-rich

production.cycle_time_description: Hours to days depending on resin system and part size. Room-temperature epoxy cures in 12-24 hours; post-cure adds several hours at 60-80C.

advantages: Lowest equipment cost of any composites process
No special tooling or facility required
Very flexible geometry — almost any open shape
Easy to learn — ideal starting point for beginners
Wide range of compatible fibre and resin types
Ideal for prototypes and one-off parts
limitations: Low fibre volume fraction (35-50%)
Inconsistent quality — highly operator-dependent
High void content compared to other processes
20-40% lower mechanical properties than autoclave prepreg with same materials
Difficult to control thickness precisely
Styrene emissions with polyester/vinyl-ester resins
typical_applications: Car body kits and cosmetic fairings

processes.name: Vacuum Bagging
processes.description: Wet layup or dry fabric sealed under a flexible bag with vacuum applied to compact the laminate, remove trapped air, and squeeze out excess resin. Applies approximately 1 atm (0.1 MPa) of uniform pressure.

capabilities.surface_quality_notes: Mould side is excellent; bag side is smooth but shows breather texture

cost.consumables_note: Peel ply, release film, bleeder, breather, bag film, sealant tape are single-use per cure cycle

production.cycle_time_description: Similar to wet layup cure time plus 30-60 min for bag setup. Vacuum held throughout cure.

advantages: Significant quality improvement over wet layup at low additional cost
Higher fibre volume fraction (50-55%) through compaction
Lower void content — atmospheric pressure drives out trapped air
More consistent laminate thickness
Compatible with oven post-cure for better mechanical properties
Same flexible geometry capability as wet layup
limitations: Higher consumables cost per cycle (bag, breather, bleeder are single-use)
Requires leak-free bag seal — corners and fittings are common failure points
Longer setup time than open-mould wet layup
Limited to ~0.1 MPa compaction pressure
Operator skill required for consistent bagging
typical_applications: Small marine structures and boat repairs
Sporting goods — bicycle frames, skis, kayak paddles

processes.name: Resin Infusion / VARTM
processes.description: Dry fabric stacked on mould, sealed under vacuum bag, then liquid resin is pulled through the stack by vacuum. Achieves near-prepreg quality at near-wet-layup material cost.

capabilities.surface_quality_notes: Mould side excellent; bag side is resin-rich but smoother than wet layup

suitable_materials.resin_requirements: Low viscosity (<300-500 mPa.s), adequate pot life for part size, low exotherm

cost.consumables_note: Flow media, spiral tubing, bag film, sealant tape, catch pot — single-use per infusion

production.cycle_time_description: Dry layup: 1-4 hours depending on size. Infusion: 30 min to 3 hours. Cure: 6-24 hours room temp, or 2-4 hours oven.

advantages: High fibre volume fraction (50-60%) at low material cost
Dry layup is faster and cleaner than wet layup
Excellent for very large parts — boat hulls, wind turbine blades
Visible flow front allows real-time monitoring
Low VOC emissions — closed system keeps resin contained
Good repeatability with established inlet/outlet strategy
limitations: Requires low-viscosity infusion-grade resin
Race-tracking and dry spots are common failure modes if inlet/outlet placement is wrong
Not ideal for very thick laminates (>20-25 mm) — resin may gel before full wet-out
Setup overhead makes it inefficient for very small parts
One-shot process — if infusion fails, the part is scrap
Flow simulation recommended for complex parts
typical_applications: Large automotive panels and truck fairings

processes.name: RTM (Resin Transfer Moulding)
processes.description: Dry fibre preform placed in a rigid closed mould (matched tooling). Resin injected under positive pressure (1-10 bar). Both surfaces are mould-quality. Higher cost tooling but excellent repeatability and surface finish.

capabilities.surface_quality_notes: Both surfaces are mould-quality (class A possible). Excellent for visible/cosmetic parts.

suitable_materials.resin_requirements: Low to medium viscosity, fast gel times preferred for production rate

production.cycle_time_description: 10-60 minutes per part for injection and cure (fast-cure resins). Preform preparation adds time but can be done offline.

part_geometry.notes: Can produce ribs, bosses, and integral stiffeners within the mould

advantages: Excellent dimensional accuracy — both surfaces are mould-defined
Class A surface finish possible on both sides
High repeatability — low part-to-part variation
Low void content with proper process control
Short cycle times possible with fast-cure resins (HP-RTM: 2-5 min)
Net-shape or near-net-shape parts reduce post-processing
limitations: High tooling cost — matched metal moulds are expensive
Part size limited by mould and press capacity (typically <5 m2)
Tooling lead time is long (weeks to months)
Mould clamping force required — need a press or robust clamping system
Not economical for low volumes (<100 parts) due to tooling amortisation
Limited thickness variation within a single part
typical_applications: Automotive body panels and structural parts (BMW i3, Lamborghini)
Small-to-medium structural components with cosmetic requirements

processes.name: Prepreg Hand Layup + Oven Cure
processes.description: Pre-impregnated fibre (prepreg) laid up by hand and cured in an oven under vacuum-only pressure (~0.1 MPa). Uses out-of-autoclave (OOA) prepreg systems designed to consolidate without autoclave pressure.

capabilities.surface_quality_notes: Mould side is excellent; bag side is very good. Slightly lower quality than autoclave due to lower compaction pressure.

suitable_materials.resin_requirements: Out-of-autoclave (OOA) prepreg formulations designed for vacuum-only cure

cost.notes: Prepreg material cost is 2-5x higher than dry fabric + resin. Freezer storage required (-18C).

production.cycle_time_description: Layup: 2-8 hours depending on part complexity. Debulk every 3-5 plies (15 min each). Oven cure: 2-6 hours at 80-180C depending on resin system.

advantages: Near-autoclave quality without autoclave capital cost
Precise, factory-controlled resin content — low part-to-part variation
Clean layup process — no liquid resin mixing on the shop floor
Better mechanical properties than wet layup or infusion
Accessible to smaller companies without autoclave infrastructure
Can process very large parts that would not fit in an autoclave
limitations: Prepreg material is 2-5x more expensive than dry fabric + resin
Requires freezer storage (-18C) — limited shelf life and out-time
Slightly lower compaction than autoclave — marginally higher void content
OOA-specific prepreg systems required (not all prepregs work vacuum-only)
Manual layup is slow for large or complex parts
Debulking between ply groups adds cycle time
typical_applications: Motorsport structures (F1, WEC — bodywork, aero packages)
Small aircraft primary and secondary structures
High-performance sporting goods (tennis rackets, golf shafts, bicycle frames)
Tooling and moulds for composite production
Large structures that exceed autoclave capacity (wind turbine spars, large fairings)

processes.name: Prepreg + Autoclave
processes.description: Pre-impregnated fibre laid up (by hand or automation), vacuum-bagged, then cured in an autoclave under combined heat (120-180C) and pressure (0.3-0.7 MPa). The gold standard for composite quality — delivers the highest fibre volume fraction, lowest void content, and best repeatability.

capabilities.surface_quality_notes: Both surfaces excellent. Mould side is class A. Bag side is very smooth under autoclave pressure.

cost.notes: Autoclave purchase price dominates capital cost. Energy cost per cure cycle is significant. Tooling must withstand autoclave pressure and temperature.

production.cycle_time_description: Layup: 4-40 hours for complex parts. Debulk every 3-5 plies. Autoclave cycle: 4-12 hours including heat-up, dwell, and cool-down.
production.automation_notes: AFP/ATL often used for layup; cure is always autoclave

advantages: Highest achievable composite quality — <1% void content
Highest fibre volume fraction (55-65%) of any layup process
Most repeatable mechanical properties — essential for certification
Proven for primary aerospace structures (wings, fuselage, empennage)
Factory-controlled resin content eliminates mixing variability
Extensive material qualification database (allowables)
limitations: Extremely high capital cost — autoclave alone costs $500k-$10M+
High energy consumption per cure cycle
Part size limited by autoclave chamber dimensions
Prepreg requires freezer storage and has limited out-time
Long cure cycles — 4-12 hours per load
Tooling must withstand autoclave pressure and temperature (expensive materials)
Highest overall cost per kilogram of finished composite
typical_applications: Commercial aircraft primary structure (wing skins, fuselage barrels, spars)

processes.name: AFP (Automated Fibre Placement)
processes.description: Robotic head places multiple narrow prepreg tows (3.175-12.7 mm each) simultaneously onto a tool surface. Each tow can be independently started, stopped, and cut. Capable of following complex curved surfaces with high precision.

capabilities.surface_quality_notes: Depends on cure method. Autoclave-cured AFP parts have excellent surface quality.

cost.notes: Capital cost dominates. Programming and path planning add significant non-recurring engineering cost.

production.cycle_time_description: Layup rate: 5-30 kg/hr depending on part geometry and machine. Complex parts with many tow drops/adds are slower. Cure time depends on method (autoclave or OOA).

part_geometry.notes: Excels on complex contoured surfaces. Tow steering allows geodesic and non-geodesic fibre paths. Limited by minimum steering radius.

advantages: Handles complex 3D contoured surfaces with high precision
Individual tow control allows complex ply boundaries and tailored layups
Excellent repeatability — machine accuracy ±1 mm position, ±1 deg angle
Lower material waste than hand layup (tows placed precisely where needed)
Full traceability — machine records every tow position
Scalable — can lay up very large structures (fuselage barrels, wing skins)
limitations: Very high capital cost ($2-10M per machine)
Significant programming and path planning effort for each new part
Lower deposition rate on complex geometry than ATL on flat parts
Minimum steering radius limits fibre path options
Tow gaps and overlaps at course boundaries affect structural properties
Requires skilled technicians for machine operation and maintenance
typical_applications: Rocket motor cases and payload fairings

processes.name: ATL (Automated Tape Laying)
processes.description: Robotic gantry or CNC machine lays wide prepreg tape (75-300 mm) onto flat or gently curved tool surfaces. Highest deposition rate of any automated layup process for suitable geometries.

capabilities.surface_quality_notes: Uniform tape laydown gives very consistent surface. Final quality depends on cure method.

cost.notes: Highest deposition rate of any composites layup process on flat/gently curved surfaces.

production.cycle_time_description: Layup rate: 15-60 kg/hr on flat geometry. Very fast for large flat panels. Cure time depends on autoclave or oven cycle.

part_geometry.notes: Best for large, flat or gently single-curved surfaces. Wide tape cannot conform to double curvature without wrinkling.

advantages: Highest deposition rate of any composites layup process (up to 60 kg/hr)
Excellent for large flat or gently curved panels
Very consistent ply thickness and fibre alignment
Low material waste on rectangular/regular geometries
Full machine traceability of every tape course
Lower programming complexity than AFP for suitable geometries
limitations: Cannot handle double curvature or complex contours — wide tape wrinkles
High capital cost ($2-8M)
Limited to wide prepreg tape as input material
Not suitable for small parts — machine footprint is very large
Complex ply boundaries require cutting and repositioning, reducing efficiency
Cannot steer tape — only straight or gently curved paths
typical_applications: Large panel layups for subsequent forming (hot drape forming)
Composite floor panels and deck structures

processes.name: Filament Winding
processes.description: Continuous fibre (wet with resin or as towpreg) wound under tension around a rotating mandrel in precise, programmable patterns. Dominant process for pressure vessels, pipes, and axisymmetric structures.

capabilities.surface_quality_notes: Outer surface shows fibre pattern (band marks). Inner surface defined by mandrel — can be very smooth.

cost.notes: Mandrel cost varies enormously — reusable steel mandrels for pipes vs expendable/dissolvable mandrels for enclosed vessels.

production.cycle_time_description: Simple pipes: minutes. Pressure vessels: 1-8 hours. Cure: room temp to oven depending on resin system.

part_geometry.notes: Best for surfaces of revolution — cylinders, cones, spheres, domes. Non-axisymmetric shapes are possible but limited.

advantages: Highest fibre volume fraction of any composites process (55-70%)
Very low material waste — continuous fibre, no cutting
Excellent repeatability — CNC-controlled winding patterns
High production rate for suitable geometries (pipes in minutes)
Lower capital cost than AFP/ATL ($100k-$1M vs $2-10M)
Wide range of fibre and resin compatibility
Well-established design methods (netting analysis, geodesic paths)
limitations: Limited to surfaces of revolution or near-axisymmetric shapes
Cannot place fibres in arbitrary directions — limited to continuous paths
Ply drop-offs and local reinforcements are very difficult
Outer surface shows winding pattern — not cosmetically smooth
Mandrel design and extraction can be complex for enclosed shapes
Concave surfaces cause fibre bridging
typical_applications: Hydrogen and CNG pressure vessels (Type III, IV, V)
Rocket motor cases and solid propellant casings
Industrial pipes and ducting (oil/gas, chemical, water)
Composite utility poles and tubular structures

processes.name: Pultrusion
processes.description: Continuous fibres pulled through a resin bath then through a heated steel die that shapes and cures the profile in one continuous operation. Produces constant cross-section profiles at high speed and low cost.

capabilities.surface_quality_notes: Die-defined surface is smooth and consistent. Can achieve Class A finish with polished dies.

cost.notes: Lowest cost per metre of any composites process for constant cross-section profiles. Die cost is the main tooling investment.

production.cycle_time_description: Continuous process — pull speed 0.3-3.0 m/min depending on cross-section and resin. Runs 24/7 in production.

part_geometry.notes: ONLY constant cross-section profiles (I-beams, angles, channels, tubes, rods, flat strips). Cannot produce varying geometry along the length.

advantages: Lowest cost per unit length for constant cross-section composites
Very high fibre volume fraction (50-70%) due to die compaction
Continuous production — high throughput, 24/7 operation possible
Extremely low material waste (<5%)
Excellent dimensional consistency over long production runs
Low labour requirement — highly automated
Wide range of profile shapes (I, C, L, T, tube, rod, custom)
limitations: ONLY constant cross-section parts — no taper, no thickness change, no curvature
Limited to predominantly 0-degree fibres (along pull direction) — transverse properties are lower
Adding off-axis fibres (mat, woven, braided) reduces pull speed and increases cost
High die tooling cost — economical only at high volumes
Profile length limited only by handling and transport
Cannot integrate features like bosses, ribs, or inserts during process
typical_applications: Structural profiles for construction (I-beams, channels, angles)
Wind turbine spar caps (flat pultruded strips stacked)
Rebar and dowel bars for concrete reinforcement
Composite utility poles and light standards

comparison_notes.quality_ranking_note: Ranked by typical void content and fibre volume fraction. Pultrusion ranks lower in this general list but achieves excellent properties in the fibre direction for its specific profile applications.
comparison_notes.cost_ranking_note: Ranked by total cost per kg for low-to-medium volume production. At very high volumes, automated processes (pultrusion, filament winding, RTM) become the cheapest per-part options despite higher capital cost.
comparison_notes.process_selection_guidance: Process selection depends on: (1) part geometry — axisymmetric favours winding, constant cross-section favours pultrusion, complex surfaces favour AFP; (2) production volume — low volume favours manual processes, high volume favours automation; (3) performance requirements — aerospace primary structure needs autoclave prepreg, industrial parts can use infusion or RTM; (4) budget — both capital and per-part cost matter.
